splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity trumps Auer/Kisor deference to agency interpretations of ambiguous provisions in the Sentencing Guidelines when the interpretation expands criminal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether courts should defer to the Sentencing Commission's commentary interpreting Guidelines provisions in a manner that increases criminal penalties, or whether the rule of lenity should take priority over such deference. This matters because it determines how ambiguous sentencing enhancements are resolved and directly affects defendants' sentences.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes priority over Auer/Kisor deference to the Sentencing Commission's commentary, meaning ambiguous Guidelines provisions should be construed in defendants' favor rather than deferring to anti-defendant agency interpretations.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that courts should defer to the Sentencing Commission's commentary under Auer/Kisor deference even when the interpretation expands criminal liability, effectively displacing the rule of lenity in the Guidelines context.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' in U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses like conspiracy, such that Application Note 1 (which includes conspiracy) is not entitled to Stinson/Kisor deference.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether Application Note 1 to the career-offender guideline, which adds conspiracy and other inchoate offenses to the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is a permissible interpretation of an ambiguous guideline or an impermissible expansion of clear text. This affects whether defendants with prior conspiracy convictions qualify for the career-offender enhancement, significantly increasing their sentencing ranges.

positions.label: Commentary is entitled to deference
positions.summary: Holds that the definition of 'controlled substance offense' is ambiguous and Application Note 1's inclusion of inchoate offenses is a reasonable interpretation entitled to controlling weight under Stinson and Kisor.

positions.label: Commentary exceeds guideline text
positions.summary: Holds that the text of § 4B1.2(b) unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses and Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the guideline beyond its plain meaning, so it is not entitled to deference.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any one criterion is disqualifying).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether defendants must meet all three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) to be disqualified from safety-valve relief, or whether meeting any single criterion is sufficient. This split directly affects mandatory minimum sentences for drug offenders and creates geographic disparities in sentencing.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), reading 'and' in its ordinary conjunctive sense.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) is sufficient to disqualify a defendant from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' as 'or' based on context and structure.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state schedule includes substances not listed in the federal Controlled Substances Act.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires the underlying substance to be federally controlled or whether any state-law drug offense qualifies. This affects base offense levels and career-offender determinations for defendants with prior state drug convictions.

positions.label: State-law offenses qualify regardless of federal scheduling
positions.summary: Holds that 'controlled substance offense' under § 4B1.2(b) broadly includes offenses under state law, even if the particular substance is not controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act, because there is no textual basis to graft a federal limitation onto the guideline.

positions.label: Substance must be federally controlled
positions.summary: Holds that a prior state conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' only if the substance at issue is also controlled under federal law, requiring a categorical or modified categorical match to federal schedules.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the First Step Act's non-retroactive anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c) can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A), and whether the Sentencing Commission's policy statement purporting to allow it exceeds the Commission's authority.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether courts may consider non-retroactive changes in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's elimination of mandatory stacked § 924(c) sentences, as grounds for compassionate release. Some circuits hold the Commission can authorize this via policy statements, while others hold that non-retroactive changes cannot contribute to extraordinary and compelling reasons and that the Commission lacks authority to override this. This affects hundreds of prisoners serving decades-long stacked sentences.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in law, whether alone or combined with other factors, cannot constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for sentence reduction under § 3582(c)(1)(A), and the Sentencing Commission's policy statement to the contrary exceeds its statutory authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that courts may consider non-retroactive changes in sentencing law, including the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment, as part of the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis, particularly when combined with other factors or when the Commission's policy statement authorizes it.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners challenging BOP decisions about the terms and conditions of confinement — such as eligibility for prerelease custody under the First Step Act — must proceed via habeas corpus under 28 U.S.C. § 2241 or may bring claims under civil rights statutes like Bivens or the APA.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists over whether challenges to the conditions or execution of a federal prisoner's confinement (as opposed to the fact or duration of confinement) must be brought as habeas corpus petitions or may be brought as civil rights actions. This matters because habeas requires exhaustion of administrative remedies and limits available relief, while civil rights claims offer broader remedies including damages.

positions.label: Habeas is the exclusive remedy for execution-of-sentence claims
positions.summary: Holds that claims challenging the execution of a sentence, including BOP decisions about prerelease custody and earned time credits, must be brought via habeas corpus under § 2241 and cannot be pursued through civil rights actions.

positions.label: Civil rights claims are available for conditions challenges
positions.summary: Holds that prisoners may bring civil rights claims for challenges to conditions of confinement that do not directly contest the fact or duration of imprisonment, even when habeas might also be available.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may consider punishment as a purpose when revoking supervised release and imposing a sentence for a violation, or whether revocation sentences must be limited to the purposes specified in 18 U.S.C. § 3583(e).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether punishment is a permissible consideration at supervised release revocation proceedings. The Sixth Circuit has held that courts may expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release, while other circuits interpret the statutory text as limiting revocation sentences to deterrence, public protection, rehabilitation, and correctional treatment. This affects sentencing for the large number of federal defendants whose supervised release is revoked each year.

positions.label: Punishment is permissible
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release, even though the statute does not list punishment among the permissible purposes of revocation sentences.

positions.label: Punishment is not a permissible purpose
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release revocation sentences must serve only the statutory purposes of deterrence, public protection, rehabilitation, and correctional treatment — not punishment — because Congress deliberately omitted punishment from § 3583(e).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether actuaries must finalize assumptions before the plan year ends or may adopt assumptions after the measurement date. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for employers participating in multiemployer pension plans, as the timing of assumption selection directly controls withdrawal liability calculations.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that actuarial assumptions used to calculate withdrawal liability must be determined as of the statutory measurement date and cannot be selected after that date, providing employers with greater predictability.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that plan actuaries may adopt or change actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, allowing them to use the most current information available when calculating withdrawal liability.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sofamor Danek Group v. Brown Group

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether federal courts may apply a judicially created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the supervision period beyond the term specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects sentencing calculations at revocation hearings for thousands of individuals who abscond each year and raises fundamental questions about judicial power to create doctrines that extend punishment without explicit statutory authorization.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled during periods of absconding, so that the supervision period is extended by the time the supervisee was a fugitive, allowing revocation proceedings even after the nominal term has expired.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that there is no statutory basis for tolling supervised release during absconding, and courts lack authority to judicially create a tolling doctrine that extends the term of supervision beyond what Congress specified.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under 28 U.S.C. § 2255.
splits.description: A 6-to-3 circuit split exists on whether federal prisoners face a categorical bar under § 2244(b)(1) against raising any claim they previously presented in a successive § 2255 motion. If (b)(1) applies, federal prisoners must overcome both § 2244(b)(1)'s absolute bar and § 2255(h)'s requirements. If it does not, they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of new evidence or a new constitutional rule.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s bar on previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, imposing an additional gatekeeping requirement beyond § 2255(h).

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s absolute bar on previously raised claims does not apply to federal prisoners' § 2255 motions, so they need only satisfy the requirements of § 2255(h).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of a debtor's asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor upon good-faith conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value between the filing of a Chapter 13 petition and conversion to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor. This directly affects debtors' ability to retain their homes and other appreciating assets when they must convert from reorganization to liquidation.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that the plain language of § 348(f)(1)(A), combined with § 541(a)'s broad definition of estate property, means that post-petition appreciation inures to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion, not the debtor.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that the Bankruptcy Code as a whole, including § 348(f)(1)(A)'s structure, legislative history, and policy of protecting good-faith converting debtors, establishes that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation belongs to the debtors, not the estate.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the appeal deadline for a Hyde Amendment attorney's fees order is governed by the civil timeline (60 days when the government is a party) or the criminal timeline (14 days) under the Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil or criminal matter for purposes of the appellate deadline. This matters because mischaracterizing the applicable deadline can result in dismissal of an appeal as untimely.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the civil appeal deadline applies, joining the majority view in a lopsided circuit split.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion arises within and is part of the criminal case, so the 14-day criminal appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b) applies.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal documents containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine.
splits.description: Circuits have taken different approaches to whether denial of sealing motions involving medical privacy constitutes a collateral order that is effectively unreviewable after final judgment. The D.C. Circuit found such orders immediately appealable given the high-order value of medical privacy, while other circuits have been more restrictive in applying the collateral order doctrine to sealing disputes.

positions.label: Immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that medical privacy is a value of sufficiently 'high order' that denial of a motion to seal medical records is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because delayed review would irrevocably compromise the privacy interest.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that sealing orders generally do not satisfy the collateral order doctrine's requirements because litigants can seek other forms of protection or challenge the order after final judgment.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits have disagreed on whether candidates can establish Article III standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures, particularly ballot-counting deadlines. The question has implications for when and how election rules can be challenged, affecting voting procedures nationwide.

positions.label: Standing exists for candidates
positions.summary: Holds that candidates have standing to challenge election rules before an election because the risk of vote dilution or competitive disadvantage constitutes a cognizable injury in fact traceable to the challenged law.

positions.label: Standing is lacking or uncertain
positions.summary: Holds that candidates lack standing to challenge election procedures when they cannot show a concrete and particularized injury, as the alleged harm is speculative before the election occurs.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The circuits have applied differing standards for evaluating discrimination claims against hospitality and business operators, leading to inconsistent results regarding liability and available remedies. SCOTUS granted cert to resolve the split, which impacts hospitality, retail, and other service industries nationwide.

positions.label: Broader liability standard
positions.summary: Applies a more expansive standard for discrimination claims against business operators, allowing broader theories of liability and remedies.

positions.label: Narrower liability standard
positions.summary: Applies a more restrictive standard that limits the scope of actionable discrimination claims and available remedies against business operators.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state law categorically barring transgender women from women's sports teams violates the Equal Protection Clause as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated sex-based biological advantages, and whether as-applied equal protection challenges are viable under intermediate scrutiny.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether categorical bans on transgender athlete participation survive intermediate scrutiny when applied to individuals who have undergone medical transition. The case also raises the broader question of whether sex-based classifications affecting transgender individuals warrant heightened scrutiny.

positions.label: Categorical ban violates Equal Protection as applied
positions.summary: Holds that a categorical ban fails intermediate scrutiny as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated biological advantages, because the state has not shown the ban is substantially related to its interest in competitive fairness for this subclass.

positions.label: Categorical ban does not violate Equal Protection
positions.summary: Holds that biological sex-based classifications in athletics are substantially related to the important governmental interest in fair competition and the safety of female athletes, even as applied to transgender women.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: B.P.J. v. West Virginia State Board of Education

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
